meta.title: Who really said "When everybody thinks alike, nobody will think at all"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No, John F. Kennedy did not coin it. This saying appeared anonymously in 1905; a variant was pinned on JFK only in 1964, after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When everybody thinks alike, nobody will think at all'?
meta.ogDescription: The exact line surfaced anonymously in a 1905 magazine filler. It was credited to JFK only in a 1964 letter — a full posthumous misattribution.

answer.label: Not John F. Kennedy — an anonymous saying from 1905
answer.authorDates: Exact wording first recorded 1905 · author unknown
answer.sourceLine: The exact line — “When everybody thinks alike, nobody will think at all” — appeared as an unsigned filler item in the Philadelphia periodical The Westminster in 1905, with no author named, according to Quote Investigator. Kennedy was credited only in 1964 — after his death — and with a different variant, so the popular attribution is unsupported.

source.excerpt: When everybody thinks alike, nobody will think at all.
trail: The earliest exact match is an anonymous filler item in The Westminster (1905), per Quote Investigator.
Walter Lippmann published the related “Where all think alike, no one thinks very much” in The Stakes of Diplomacy (1915, p. 51).

The John F. Kennedy credit appears only in a 1964 Dallas Morning News reader letter — after Kennedy’s death — and quotes a different variant, “If everyone is thinking alike, then no one is thinking at all,” per QI.
The same idea has drifted onto Benjamin Franklin and George S. Patton (both from a single 1979 book of recollections), which QI rates a “weak” attribution.
source.excerptNote: The wording most people quote. A closely related idea — “Where all think alike, no one thinks very much” — was published by journalist Walter Lippmann in 1915, but even that is a variant, not the exact line.

author.name: John F. Kennedy
author.heading: About John F. Kennedy
author.bio: John Fitzgerald Kennedy served as the 35th U.S. President from 1961 until his assassination in November 1963. A Pulitzer Prize–winning author (Profiles in Courage) and celebrated orator, he is one of the internet’s most common magnets for inspirational quotes he never uttered. There is no record of Kennedy originating this saying, which predates his public life by decades.

misattribution.heading: Why John F. Kennedy gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Kennedy is one of the internet’s default attributions for punchy, freedom-flavored aphorisms. This one predates his career by decades and was only ever pinned on him after he died.

items.why: No Kennedy speech, book, or letter contains this line. The only Kennedy credit documented by Quote Investigator is a 1964 Dallas Morning News reader letter — published after his November 1963 death — and it quotes a different variant.
Lippmann genuinely wrote “Where all think alike, no one thinks very much” in The Stakes of Diplomacy (1915), but that is a distinct wording published a decade after the anonymous 1905 line.
Both trace to Porter B. Williamson’s 1979 book of Patton recollections, not to any primary source; QI calls the Patton link “weak.”

misattribution.truthLine: The exact line is an anonymous 1905 saying — not Kennedy, not Lippmann, not Franklin or Patton.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The thought is old and communal. As early as 1865, Dr. Henry Gibbons told a California alumni gathering that “it is the unthinking people…who think alike,” and by 1905 the crisp modern form was circulating anonymously in magazine fillers.

Because the sentiment flatters independent thinking, it has been re-credited across the twentieth century to whoever the quoter admired — Lippmann, Kennedy, Franklin, Patton. Each new famous name displaces the honest answer, which is that no single author can be shown to have coined it.
context.pull: A saying this old and this anonymous belongs to no one — least of all a president credited only after his death.
